newsitem.title: FRANCE: French markets give Jospin benefit of the doubt.
newsitem.headline: French markets give Jospin benefit of the doubt.

text.p: French financial markets climbed on Tuesday as investors took heart from encouraging remarks by the new Socialist leaders and a perception that European monetary union would start on time with a large number of countries.

The franc, bond and interest rate futures were all higher on Tuesday, boosted by Socialist comments that they would stick to the timetable for a single European currency and relief in Germany that a row over revaluing gold reserves was settled.

The CAC-40 index of blue-chip stocks settled up 0.89 percent at 2,624.49, building on Monday's 0.68 percent gain, as investors reasoned that in practice the change in government would not adversely affect most companies' prospects.

"The fundamentals are good, and we have to stay calm," said Jean Laurent Bruel, fund manager at Banque Sifas. "Just because there's a change in government, companies aren't going to stop making profits. We have to seize opportunities."
Brokers said the stock market looked cheap after its 6.5 percent fall last week on indications that the left would win the parliamentary elections on Sunday.

"The market's taking a gamble, giving credit to (Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin that he will not shake up Europe, and, as the (stock) market is cheap, people are buying," an equity trader in Paris said.
Retail stocks continued to climb on the Paris bourse on hopes that a Socialist push for faster growth and boost to purchasing power would increase lacklustre French consumption.
Among French retailers, Promodes rose 3.87 percent and Eridania Beghin-Say added 3.13 percent. Dollar stocks were helped by the U.S. currency's gain with Elf Aquitaine up 3.17 percent.

Encouraging noises from the Socialists also helped Monday's biggest losers - financial companies and stocks involved in the now uncertain French privatisation programme - to rebound. Lagardere, a bidder for state defence electronics firm Thomson-CSF, rose 4.47 percent.

A Socialist-led government, relying on Communist support, was initially seen as a worst-case scenario on the grounds the anti-Maastricht Communists could spark rifts with Germany and ultimately cause the whole project to be delayed.
Analysts said Elisabeth Guigou, tipped to serve as the Socialists' European Affairs minister, had helped reassure bond and equity markets on Tuesday morning.

Guigou said the new left government would keep to the timetable for launching a single European currency and while the Communists would be welcome in government their participation should not be tied to conditions, notably a call for a 1,000 franc rise in the minimum wage.

Philippe Brossard, head of research at ABN Amro Finance in Paris, said he was still concerned about Socialist calls for new talks on the so-called stability pact, designed to ensure countries in a single currency zone keep deficits under control.
"The Socialists are in a state of grace but they've said they won't ratify the stability pact and the market is completely ignoring this," Brossard said.

French 10-year bond yields ended Tuesday 13 basis points lower than equivalent yields in Germany. French interest rate futures climbed as much as 14 basis points, trimming implied three month interest rates to 3.47 percent from a 1997 high of 3.88 percent touched last week.

The franc fell to a year's low of 3.3860 per mark after the election results but a slide in the German unit against other major currencies pushed the franc back towards 3.37. It was trading at 3.3720 per mark at 1630 GMT, about one centime short of a four-year high hit in late April.
